In this lesson you will learn about diode clampers. This is a circuit application for the diode.
INTRODUCTIONM
Clampers are so named because they change the voltage level of an AC signal by adding a DC voltage.
They are useful, simple circuits, consisting of a diode, resistor and a capacitor.
Clampers are used in televisions to add a DC voltage to the video signal for operation of the picture tube.
Clampers are used in any circuit where an AC signal must ride on a DC level.
Let's begin the lesson on DIODE CLAMPER OPERATION.........................
LESSON MENU
The purpose of a diode clamper is to clamp an AC input signal at a DC output level.
DISCUSSION
The AC signal can be changed so either the positive or negative peak is at 0 V.
The peaks can also be placed above or below 0V.
A clamper's effect on an input signal depends on how circuit components are connected.
The operation of each circuit is based on the action of a junction diode.
A forward biased diode conducts, acting almost like a short circuit.
A forward biased diode conducts, acting almost like a short circuit.
FORWARD BIASED DIODE - Forward biased diodes have a very small voltage drop due to the barrier junction. A germanium diode drops approximately .3 V; a silicon diode drops approximately .7 V.
A reverse biased diode is cutoff, acting like an open circuit.
By placing the diode in different configurations, different output signals are produced.
The two basic configurations of diode clampers are:........
A positive clamper has the diode pointing up or towards the output signal. Positive clampers add a positive DC voltage.
When the diode is forward biased, the path for AC current is through the low resistance of the diode to ground.
When the diode is reversed biased, the path for AC current is through the high resistance of the resistor.
Foward biased diode - Low Resistence allows current flow
Reverse biased diode - High Resistence allows current flow
CHARGING AND DISCHARGING OF A CAPACITOR - The charging and discharging of a capacitor depends on the RC time constant: TC = C x R.
The value of the capacitor does not change in a clamper circuit. The diode affects circuit resistance which determines the time constant.
An input signal's negative alternation forward biases the diode.
The capacitor quickly charges to the peak value with the positive polarity on the output.
Adding the +Vp on the capacitor to the -Vp of the input signal produces a half cycle output with 0 V at the negative peak.
The positive charge on the capacitor raised the voltage level of the output signal.
An input signal's positive alternation reverse biases the diode.
The capacitor does not have time to discharge through the resistor. The positive voltage on the capacitor remains.
Adding the +Vp on the capacitor to the +Vp of the input signal produces twice the output.
The positive charge on the capacitor raised the voltage level of the output signal.
The peak to peak value of the output signal does not change, only the DC level.
Remember, the diode action allows the capacitor to charge quickly through low resistance and discharge slowly through high resistance. The capacitor charges but does not discharge.
Remember, the diode action allows the capacitor to charge quickly through low resistance and discharge slowly through high resistance. The capacitor charges but does not discharge.
Remember, the positive voltage on the capacitor is added to the input signal.
The negative clamper operates the same except a negative DC voltage is added.
A negative clamper has the diode pointing down or towards ground. A negative clamper adds a negative voltage to the output.
During the positive alternation the diode is forward biased. The capacitor quickly charges to the peak value with the negative polarity on the output.
Adding the -Vp on the capacitor to the +Vp of the input signal produces a half cycle output with 0V at the positive peak.
During the negative alternation, the diode is reverse biased. The capacitor does not have time to discharge through the resistor.
Adding the -Vp on the capacitor to the -Vp of the input signal produces twice the output.
The peak to peak value of the output signal does not change, only the DC level.
Remember, the capacitor is allowed to charge but not discharge and the negative voltage on the capacitor is added to the input signal.

An unbiased clamper clamps either the negative peak at 0 volts (positive clamper) or the positive peak at 0 volts (negative clamper).
TRY AGAIN!
By adding circuit bias, the voltage level of the peaks are changed from 0 V.
A positive bias on a positive clamper raises the output voltage DC level.
The peak to peak input and output voltage is still 10V, but the negative peak was raised to the level of the bias voltage.
A negative bias on a positive clamper lowers the output voltage DC level.
The peak to peak input and output voltage is still 10V, but the negative peak was lowered to the level of the bias voltage.
A negative bias on a positive clamper lowers the output voltage DC level.
A positive bias on a negative clamper raises the output voltage DC level.
The peak to peak input and output voltage is still 10V, but the positive peak was raised to the level of the bias voltage.
A negative bias on a negative clamper lowers the output voltage DC level.
The peak to peak input and output voltage is still 10V, but the positive peak was lowered to the level of the bias voltage.
Remember, a biased clamper works just like an unbiased clamper.
The bias either raises (positive bias) or lowers (negative bias) the DC level.
